header.lede: Every id-stable interface works — until trees get big or sessions get long. Then only anchored patches do, and they barely need to see the tree. Finding where to look costs one search call, and remembering the session costs two worked examples plus a memo — even 36 edits in. And the view is a correctness contract: what the model must read, it must be shown. Views carry values; memos carry goals — the agent can be trusted to write the memo itself, and "undo that" needs an echo, not a transcript. The standing brand pack simply works — and when a rule collides with a request, models pick a reading rather than break either; our first claim about WHICH reading was refuted by its own confirmation study a day later. And the series-long villain fell last: offered one sentence of permission, every model asked instead of guessing, 270/270 — the silence was protocol, not blindness. Then the whole core stack was re-run on the tier the downstream surfaces actually ship, claude-opus-4.8, and every gate passed: the frontier does not need the training wheels, though they cost nothing to keep. And when we probed the ask path for its breaking point, the tax was zero and the answer loop was perfect; the one crack is that below the frontier tier, models silently resolve ambiguous references instead of asking about them. And the one clause we had shipped on faith got its audit: making the model restate a goal it read does nothing, because where a goal comes from matters more than whether the model says it aloud. And the memo passed its stress test everywhere but one place: filled to its twenty-note cap, it silently throws away exactly the thing it exists to remember. Then we measured the obvious fix for the ambiguity gap, and it rescued the model we do not run while adding nothing to the one we do; some gaps are capabilities, not prompts. The last border closed with fine print: the ask sentence covers dangling references on every tier, and its zero tax turns out to presume the very view contract it rides along with. And the oldest habit in the protocol got its control group at last: told nothing but "that was invalid," the models fixed their patches anyway. The error message was for us, not them.
header.provenance: Main study: 200 seeded tasks × 6 conditions × 4 models × 2 regimes, temperature 0 (July 2026), plus follow-up studies G (tool-history footgun), H (300–1000-node size extension), I/J (focused views: partial-context patches, JSON and HTML renderings), K (12-edit sessions under four serialization policies), L/N (grounding without ids, then the retrieval ladder), M/O/P (session memory, positional views, synthetic history), Q/R (fan-out edits and their fixes), S (36-edit long sessions), T (conversation-carried context), U (document-carried dependencies), V (qualitative rewrites — the series' first judge-graded study, disclosed as its own track), W (agent-maintained memo extraction, the shipped mechanism verbatim, with claude-opus-4.8 as a third tier), X (edit-anaphora: amend, repeat, and undo follow-ups racing four context carriers), and Y (naturalistic extraction: twin sessions isolating declaration phrasing, with chatter bait for the noise metric). All numbers below are protocol-v2 corrected — the original interface-reliability gaps were an artifact of conversation histories that hid the model's own tool calls (vercel/ai#16840). Charts show parity prompts, models pooled unless noted; Wilson 95% intervals. Conditions: A HTML + whole-tree rewrite, B JSON + rewrite, C JSON + mutation tools, D HTML + tools, E JSON Patch, F id-anchored patch (pre-registered addendum, BRIEF-F.md), and AD (the Opus confirmation: the core stack re-run verbatim on claude-opus-4.8, 1,160 cells), and AE (the calibration ladder: five ambiguity levels plus the ask-answer-resume loop, 720 cells), and AF (restate-before-rewrite, judge-graded: 270 contemporaneous edits, both judges re-calibrated 100/100), and AH (memo saturation: recall, rules, and full-replace integrity at the shipped 20-note cap, 270 cells), and AI (the multiplicity hatch: the amended ask sentence vs the shipped one across the full ladder, 450 cells), and AG (the anaphora hatch: the shipped ask sentence on the undo-that construction plus the echo-tax co-check, 1,296 session steps), and AJ (the correction loop in isolation: seeded failures, structured vs codes vs bare feedback, 405 cells), and AK (eviction validation: the goal-preserving eviction re-measured at the Study AH injury site, 120 cells), and AL (the prompt-side fence: an anti-self-eviction sentence vs the AK-eviction arm as contemporaneous control, the prompt rule the only variable, 120 cells), and AM (consolidation-on-notice: an invitation appended to the app's eviction notice, the notice string the only variable, on a fresh 40-task cap-edge corpus, 240 cells).

sections.eyebrow: H2 · task success by tree size
sections.title: At benchmark sizes (5–150 nodes), no interface dominates
sections.takeaway: Whole-tree rewrite (A, B) leads granular tools (C, D) at every size tested. The gap peaks on small/medium trees and narrows — but never reverses — at ~150 nodes. JSON Patch (E) collapses to 69.6% on large trees — and the pre-registered addendum condition F (id-anchored patches) recovers it exactly to rewrite level at the lowest token cost.

sections.title: Corrected: multi-turn reference edits are near-parity
sections.takeaway: Success on “insert a node, then edit it by the id from your own output” — protocol v2. With the model's own tool history visible, every interface is near-parity (A 88.1% vs C 91.3%, n.s.); gemini's residual tools deficit is phase-1 editing accuracy, not follow-up dropout. Zero id-reference failures in any arm, ever. The dramatic v1 gaps live in the footgun chart below.

sections.title: Rewrite is cheap where trees are small; HTML is the terser artifact where they're large
sections.takeaway: Tools arms (C, D) resend a growing conversation every call, so they burn 4–5× more tokens on small/medium trees. At ~150 nodes the whole-artifact arms grow too — and the HTML dialect (A, 15.6k) undercuts JSON rewrite (B, 23.0k) by ~30%: the one place the format measurably matters.

sections.eyebrow: Overall · success per model × condition (parity, 200 tasks each)
sections.title: Frontier models don't care; smaller models do
sections.takeaway: Per-cell task success. Down the sonnet-4.5 and gpt-5.4 rows the interface barely matters; down the haiku-4.5 and gemini-3.5-flash rows the tools arms give up 10–17 points against rewrite.

sections.title: One hidden SDK default, two very different benchmarks
sections.takeaway: The original +33pp multi-turn gap was manufactured by conversation histories that omitted the model's own tool calls (the AI SDK v5→v7 response.messages trap). Same tasks, same prompts — only history construction differs. Under corrected history, all 2,160 Study G cells pass.

table.summary: Data table — reference-family tools success, v1 vs v2

sections.title: The crossover, found: above ~300 nodes, only anchored patches hold
sections.takeaway: Whole-tree rewrite becomes frontier-only at scale (gemini-flash: 0/15 at ~1000 nodes; sonnet needs a streaming transport and ten minutes per rewrite). Anchored patches hold 87–100% for both tiers at every size — $0.26 and 4 seconds per solved 1000-node edit. Positional patches decay to ~10%. Solid lines: sonnet-4.5; dashed: gemini-3.5-flash.

table.summary: Data table — success by model × condition × size (n = 15 per cell)

sections.title: The model doesn't need to see the tree: a ~1.5k-token view matches the full 85k-token input
sections.takeaway: Show only the path to the referenced nodes plus their child lists (everything else collapsed or omitted with a count), and anchored-patch accuracy is statistically unchanged for both models at every size — sonnet on the minimal view went 45/45 — while the view's size grows with tree depth, not node count. Rendering the view in barkup's HTML dialect instead of JSON changes nothing on accuracy (p = 1.0 in all four paired comparisons) and is 9–24% terser; it shipped as barkup/view in 0.3. Caveat: this is the oracle bound — instructions name their target ids. Solid: sonnet-4.5; dashed: gemini-3.5-flash.

table.summary: Data table — median input tokens and success by model × input × size (n = 15 per cell)

sections.title: Sessions drift unless you re-show the tree — and showing a fresh view every turn is also the cheapest policy
sections.takeaway: Twelve sequential patches against one evolving tree. Shown the tree once, sonnet decays to 83.8% by the last third (stale ordinal placements); with a fresh ~1.5k-token minimal view every turn it stays at 100% (239/240 steps) for a quarter of the tokens — the once-shown tree rides along in history every turn anyway. Whole-tree rewrite as a session protocol fails structurally: gemini silently corrupts state (all 44 failures valid-but-wrong; 2/10 sessions end intact) and one sonnet session deterministically exhausted the 200k context window at step 11. Solid: sonnet-4.5; dashed: gemini-3.5-flash.

table.summary: Data table — per-step success by session third, end-state, and mean tokens per session

sections.title: Finding the node is the expensive part: grounding costs 7–9 points, and navigation is a frontier-only trap
sections.takeaway: Same edits, instructions rewritten without ids ("the image-atom named 'maple-ember'"), every description verified to match exactly one node. With the full tree in context, models ground at 84–87% (vs 91–96% with ids). Letting the model navigate a skeleton with an expand tool matches the oracle on sonnet — at a median of 54 expansions, costing MORE than showing everything — and collapses on gemini, mostly by exhausting its budget without an answer. Naive lexical retrieval is the floor it was designed to be. The pre-registered gate failed: no partial-context mechanism was both accurate and cheaper — until Study N (next chart) swapped the expand tool for content search.

table.summary: Data table — success, input tokens, and failure anatomy by condition (45 tasks per cell)

sections.title: Stop walking, start searching: one find_nodes call grounds the edit on both model tiers
sections.takeaway: Same id-free tasks as Study L; the expand tool replaced by a single content-search tool (a few words in, the 5 best keyword matches out, shown in place). The frontier model matches its id-oracle bound exactly — same 43/45, same two failed tasks — at a median of one search call and ~90% less input; gemini jumps from 23/45 (navigating) to 39/45 (16–0 paired, p < 0.001), its full-tree score at 3% of the cost. Two more rungs: swapping the keyword matcher for text-embedding-3-small changed nothing (target coverage 23/45 vs 24/45 — embeddings can't resolve "the 3rd block inside atlas"), and two-stage grounding (gemini reads the tree, names the ids, sonnet patches a focused view) holds 41/45 with the frontier model's median input at 1,484 tokens (−97.4%). The Study L gate, re-tested, passes twice.

table.summary: Data table — success, input, and mechanism by condition (45 tasks per cell)

sections.title: The view carries the state, but history still earns its keep
sections.takeaway: If a fresh view arrives every turn, does the model need conversation history at all? No — statelessness confirmed the constant-cost economics (~1.3k input tokens at step 1 and step 12 alike) but failed the accuracy gate: sonnet lost 7 steps to 0 against full history (p = 0.016) and end-state integrity dropped from 19/20 sessions to 13–14/20, with failures concentrated in late-session placement edits. A 2-exchange window sits in between, leaning inadequate. Guidance at the time: keep the history AND the per-turn view. (Study P, two charts down, found what history was actually providing — and how to replace it.) Solid: sonnet-4.5; dashed: gemini-3.5-flash.

table.summary: Data table — per-step success by session third, end-state, and cost shape

sections.title: Printing the position on every node does not rescue stateless sessions
sections.takeaway: Study M's stateless failures were all placement edits, so Study O annotated every view child with its true 1-based position (plus a prompt line mapping ordinals to anchors) and re-ran the 2×2 of history × positions. The rescue failed: stateless accuracy moved 3–1 / 1–0 vs plain stateless (n.s.), and sessions ending byte-perfect stayed at 15/20 vs full history's 19/20 — models misplaced nodes that had the correct position printed on them. Whatever history contributes to placement, it is not arithmetic. Positions with history were descriptively the best cells in the whole series (gemini: 20/20 end-states, 60/60 late placements) but not significantly better than history alone: harmless, possibly mildly helpful, not a substitute for memory. (Study P, next chart, found the actual substitute.)

table.summary: Data table — late-session success, placement class, end-state, and cost by policy

sections.title: History was a teacher all along: two canned examples replace the whole conversation
sections.takeaway: If history isn't state (the view carries that) and isn't positional help (Study O), maybe it's worked precedent — and precedent can be faked. Two unit-tested examples (an ordinal insert and a move, on a tree the model never edits, ~900 tokens) restore stateless sessions to full-history accuracy on both models: worst paired difference vs K-view anywhere is 2–0 (n.s.), end-states back to 18–20/20, and gemini's examples arm goes 60/60 on the late placements that defined the M failure class — with 20/20 byte-perfect endings. The system-prompt framing ties the fake-turns framing, so the value is content, not conversation. Flat ~2.1k input/step forever, half of keep-history's cost at 12 edits, no context ceiling. The session guidance is revised: fresh view per turn + two worked examples in the system prompt.

table.summary: Data table — late-session success, placements, end-state, and cost by policy

sections.title: "Change every X inside Y" breaks everything — including the oracle
sections.takeaway: One instruction, 2–32 targets, on the same large trees. Even with retrieval solved (every target visible in the view), models finish only part of the set: 62–69% overall, ~45% at 7+ targets, failures 100% partial coverage. The 0.4 search recipe fails its gate (median 6 calls instead of 1; a third of runs over 100k input tokens; −24 pp vs full tree on gemini). And the series' first model inversion: sonnet is significantly better with a view (p = 0.022), gemini significantly better with the whole tree (p = 0.008) — no context strategy is model-independent here. Study R then tested the fixes: prompt-side interventions (a worked fan-out example, a coverage checklist) do NOT rescue it — but decomposition, measured directly, is perfect: the app enumerates targets and issues one single-target edit per node, 90/90 tasks on both models (674/674 subtasks, zero failures) at ~⅓ the input cost of a whole-tree prompt. The flat line at the top is the recipe. Solid: sonnet-4.5; dashed: gemini-3.5-flash.

table.summary: Data table — success by condition × target count, failure anatomy, and tokens

sections.title: 36 edits later, nothing broke — except the cost curve
sections.takeaway: Every prior session study ran 12 edits. Study S ran the two surviving recipes through 36 (10 new sessions, seed committed) and both held: full-history S-view went 719/720 steps across both models, stateless-plus-worked-examples S-system went 713/720 with no late-third decay (98–99% at steps 25–36 — step 36 is taught as well as step 1), McNemar parity everywhere, zero context ceilings, zero blocked steps. What diverges is cost: keep-history's median per-step input grows linearly to ~24k tokens by step 36 while the stateless recipe stays flat at ~2.1k, which compounds to 449k vs 81k input per session — 5.4–5.6×, against a pre-registered prediction of ≥3×. The gate passed on both models; the worked-examples recipe is the measured default for long sessions. All seven S-system step failures were placement-class (insert/move), the class Studies M/O/P mapped. Solid: sonnet-4.5; dashed: gemini-3.5-flash.

table.summary: Data table — per-third success, end-state, and tokens per session by recipe

sections.title: The one thing statelessness can't do — and the three note lines that fix it
sections.takeaway: Every prior session study used self-contained requests, so Study T built the missing class: callback steps whose required fact lives only in earlier conversation — a declared codename a later rename must use, and a standing rule later inserts must apply unprompted (validated non-derivable from every pre-step tree). The dissociation is total: the stateless worked-examples recipe fails ALL 160 callback steps (0/80 per model) while scoring 160/160 on the ordinary steps of the very same sessions. The registered fix — an app-maintained "Session notes" block, a memo instead of a transcript — recovers 80/80 on both models, ties full history on every paired comparison, beats it on end-state integrity (19–20/20 vs 17–19/20), and costs 1.02× stateless against history's 2.1×. Session guidance, final form: fresh view per turn, two worked examples, and a memo of what the user declared.

table.summary: Data table — callback and ordinary steps, end-state, and cost by arm

sections.title: The view that can't see the answer doesn't fail — it makes something up
sections.takeaway: Focused views assume the instruction carries every value an edit needs. Study U built the class where it doesn't: dependent edits ("set A's content to the same value as B's", "rename A to B's name") whose needed value is verified absent from the instruction AND from the rendered target-only view. That view failed all 90 cells across both models — and every single failure was a valid patch containing a silently invented value: zero refusals, zero invalid artifacts, 90/90 confident fictions that validate and apply. The fix is one line: put both mentioned nodes in the focus ids. That scores a perfect 90/90 — descriptively better than the whole tree, which fumbled 3 structure-reads at ~1000 nodes on sonnet — at ~1.7k median input tokens, 25× less than the full tree. The shipped search recipe can self-serve reads at 82–84% (median 2–3 calls), significantly short of full-tree parity on gemini (p = 0.008) and weakest on value-copies (75%): search grounds targets at oracle level, but reading values is the application's job. Focus ids = every node the request mentions.

table.summary: Data table — success by arm and kind, failure anatomy, and cost

sections.title: Views carry values, memos carry goals
sections.takeaway: The series' first judge-graded study, run under a pre-registered pairwise protocol: both judges (gpt-5.4 primary, haiku-4.5 sensitivity — neither an editor) first had to pass a 50-pair calibration gate with planted verdicts, identity probes, and length probes, and both aced it 50/50. The task: "rewrite this paragraph to focus on our central thesis," with the thesis planted in a mission node and the target paragraph deliberately assembled off-thesis. Five arms for where the goal lives. Blind arms lost all 120 comparisons by obliviously polishing the off-topic paragraph — fluent, valid, useless. The T memo carried the goal at full parity with an explicit instruction (sonnet's memo arm actually won 10–2 under the primary judge). The surprise that failed the gate: models with the thesis-bearing node IN THE VIEW demonstrably read it (keyword coverage +0.75 vs +0.00 blind) yet lost 117/120 — their rewrites orbit the topic where told-outright rewrites anchor the thesis. Study U's view fix moves data perfectly; it moves intent only partway. Judge agreement 83.3% (kappa 0.53); the keyword proxy ranks the arms identically. Guidance: put the nodes an edit must read in the view; put the goal in the instruction or memo, restated outright.

table.summary: Data table — win/loss/tie vs the explicit-instruction control, by arm, editor, and judge

sections.eyebrow: Study W · who writes the memo?
sections.title: The agent writes the memo faithfully — even when history makes it redundant
sections.takeaway: Studies T and V validated the memo with oracle extraction: the harness knew what to record. What ships in production delegates that judgment to the agent via an update_session_notes tool and a prompt rule, with a 32-message history window also present — and within the window, callbacks succeed via history whether or not the agent records, so a lazy agent's empty memo is invisible until truncation. Study W tested the shipped mechanism verbatim (character-identity ports) on 36-step sessions that cross the window, with a mid-session retraction, on three models including claude-opus-4.8 — the series' first data on the tier the production system runs. Both gates passed. Pure agent extraction ties the oracle exactly (recall 36/36 per model, retractions 12/12, zero noise notes, one drop event in 72 sessions), the tool gets called ~4 times per session at exactly the declarative moments, and the laziness hypothesis is refuted: with history present the recording cadence is unchanged and post-truncation callbacks hold — opus a perfect 36/36, gemini 35/36, sonnet 31/36 (not significant, and not memo-explained: its memo was complete in every failing cell). The over-32-message protection is real protection, not theater. Filled dots: post-truncation callbacks; hollow: within-window.

table.summary: Data table — callbacks by arm, window membership, memo fidelity, and cost

sections.title: "Undo that" needs an echo, not a transcript
sections.takeaway: The last structurally unmeasured request class: follow-ups that point at the previous edit — "also set that same node's…", "apply the same change to X", "actually, undo that." Anaphora steps ran against skeleton views (an oracle-focused view would leak the answer), so the carrier under test had to supply the target, the key, AND the value. Without one, no model resolves anything: 0 of 144 across sonnet, gemini, and opus, and every single failure was a valid, applied, silently guessed patch — the strongest silent-failure result in the series. Full history is near-ceiling (48/48, 48/48, 46/48). The winner is the cheapest carrier tested: a one-line last-edit echo the application appends automatically (set "key" from old to new on node), which ties history per model at about half the input cost and BEAT history outright on opus-4.8 — 48/48 against history's 46/48, with the from/to format carrying every undo on every model. Fine print, disclosed: "apply the same change to X" strains compressed carriers model-dependently (sonnet 7/12 with the echo; window-2 leaks on repeat everywhere, significantly on gemini), one more entry in the carrier-advice-is-not-model-independent ledger. The measured stateless session stack is now complete: fresh view per turn, two worked examples, the session-notes memo, and the last-edit echo.

table.summary: Data table — anaphora success by carrier, kind, and model, with failure anatomy and cost

sections.title: The memo survives how people actually talk
sections.takeaway: Every declaration in Studies T, V, and W was announced formulaically ("For later reference: the codename is X"). Real users declare mid-sentence, bury rules inside other requests, and retract with "scratch that." Study Y isolated phrasing with twin sessions: identical trees, edits, schedules, chatter, and session ids, differing ONLY in declaration rider text — one twin formulaic, one casual from registered pools. Four chatter riders per session ("the client saw a screenshot and seemed happy") gave the noise metric real bait for the first time. Both gates passed perfectly on all three models: zero discordant callback cells anywhere between casual and formulaic (every McNemar 0 to 0), recall 36 of 36 and casual retractions 12 of 12 in both stateless arms, and 432 chatter baits produced not one false memo note. Users need no announcement syntax, and the shipped record-only-declarations prompt rule is doing real discrimination work at zero false-positive cost. One disclosed whisper: under the history window, recording cadence softens at the margin (3.8 to 3.9 calls per session vs a flat 4.0 stateless), consistent with Study W's redundancy finding and covered by in-window history. The formulaic arm doubled as a clean Study W replication under added chatter.

table.summary: Data table — callbacks, recall, retractions, noise, and cadence by arm and model

sections.title: The brand pack works; the rule you forgot is the hazard
sections.takeaway: Production doc editors ship a standing context block with every request — company facts, client records, a styleguide — and nobody had measured whether models actually use it. Study Z planted machine-checkable obligations in twelve seeded org packs (~3.3k tokens: one target client, three same-schema distractors, governing rules rotated head/middle/tail among twelve styleguide rules) and raced three arms: the whole pack, an oracle-picked relevant slice, and the whole pack plus the applicable rules distilled into the session-notes memo. The core answer is emphatic: facts and rules were 216 of 216 per arm — 100% on every model in every arm — with zero cross-client contamination in 324 cells and no burial effect at any styleguide position. Slicing bought nothing on accuracy and forfeited prompt caching (the per-request slice never got a single cache read; the whole pack under the shipped cached-system layout read 64–68% of input from cache, cutting effective input cost 25–43%). The finding lives in a conflict we registered by accident: a contact-format rule written with "always" against an instruction clause asking for a product mention. Every model resolved it cleanly into one of two readings — satisfy both, or obey the format literally — with zero violations. Our first read of the split (strictness scales with capability) was REFUTED by its own pre-registered confirmation study a day later: see Study AA below. What stands from Z: distilling the rules into the memo did not change competence; it changed which reading wins (sonnet 2/12 → 11/12 satisfying both, p = 0.004). Audit your styleguide for "always" and "exactly": the failure mode of a conflicted spec is disciplined obedience to the rule you forgot you wrote.

table.summary: Data table — facts, rules, combined-cell readings, and caching by arm and model

sections.eyebrow: Study AA · conflict resolution — the confirmation study that refuted us
sections.title: We tested our own headline and lost: strictness is not a capability gradient
sections.takeaway: Study Z’s spec-conflict split was an accident with one conflict shape, so Study AA measured it on purpose: three registered conflict kinds (rule vs instruction, an explicit user countermand of a rule, rule vs rule), four arms (base, a priority meta-rule, soft “generally prefer” phrasing, rules restated in the memo tail), 432 cells. The confirmation gate predicted opus most literal and measured it LEAST literal — zero strict readings in 24 base cells against sonnet’s 10 and gemini’s 7, significant in the opposite direction (p = 0.016) — and the same conflicted template that split opus 6/6 under Z’s three-rule packs read both-obligations 12/12 under AA’s four-rule packs: which reading wins is composition-sensitive, not a model constant. The interventions: the priority meta-rule (“the user’s request takes precedence”) moved nothing significantly on any model; softening “always” to “we generally prefer” collapsed literal readings (sonnet 10/24 → 2/24, gemini 7/24 → 0/24) — the cheapest fix that works; and memo steering replicated Study Z to the digit (sonnet 2/12 → 11/12, p = 0.004) while revealing a footgun: with a rule restated in the memo, opus enforced the ™ mark against the user’s explicit “written plain, no trademark symbol” 12 of 12 times (without the memo, all 36 base cells honored the countermand). Rule-vs-rule conflicts resolved by specificity, not styleguide position. The footgun is CLOSED, measured (Study AB, 144 cells): a one-sentence precedence clause inside the memo block — the production system’s shipped mitigation, tested verbatim — restored every trampled countermand (opus 0/12 → 12/12, p = 0.0005; sonnet 3/12 → 11/12) at zero cost to the memo’s steering benefit (satisfy-both stayed 12/12 everywhere), with the injury first replicated to the digit in the control arm. The placement lesson: the same sentence class buried in the styleguide moved nothing; precedence language works at the point of injury, adjacent to the notes it governs. Across 900 conflicted cells in Z, AA, and AB: zero violations, zero contamination — models resolve conflicted specs; the conflict itself is the authoring hazard.

sections.title: The model always knew what it couldn’t see
sections.takeaway: Twenty-eight studies of silent failure (90/90 invented values in U, 144/144 silent guesses in X, 120/120 oblivious polishes in V, zero clarifying questions anywhere) never once OFFERED the model a way out. Study AC did, on Study U’s unit-validated construction: the needed value provably absent from the target-only view, provably present in the solvable twin. Two registered hatches — a one-sentence NEED-INFO prompt rule, and an ask_user tool — against a no-hatch control, 810 cells. The control replicated U exactly: 135/135 silent wrong patches. Both hatches flipped it completely: 270/270 asks on unsolvable cells, ZERO false asks and untouched solve rates on the 270 solvable twins, and every single ask named the exact missing node and attribute ("What is the content attribute value of the text-atom with id n219?"). The mechanisms were indistinguishable, so the one-sentence version is the whole result. The reframe: the models always saw the gap precisely; they guessed because the protocol demanded a patch and nothing said asking was allowed — obedience, not blindness. Guidance: ship an ask path (one sentence; wire it to a real reply mechanism), keep the context contracts (they make the question unnecessary; the hatch makes residual failures visible), and mind the disclosed caveat: this was measured at a validated hard boundary, not on merely-vague requests — calibration on fuzzy ambiguity is the follow-up. The follow-up is now measured: see the Study AE section below.

sections.title: The core stack transfers to the tier we actually ship
sections.takeaway: Studies F through U validated the core editing stack on sonnet-4.5 and gemini-3.5-flash, but the downstream template-editing surface runs claude-opus-4.8, a tier whose benchmark data began at Study W. Study Q had already shown that serializer advice inverts between models, so nothing could be assumed. Study AD re-ran the stack on opus with corpora, prompts, and graders reused verbatim: 1,160 cells, gates anchored to the weakest previously passing tier. Every gate passed, mostly at or above the top of the prior bands. The anchored-patch dialect scored 194/200 on the main corpus (the best condition-F number ever measured, and every miss was a tree-reading count question rather than an editing failure), HTML focused views swept 90/90 across 300 to 1000 nodes, search grounding landed exactly on sonnet's oracle bound (43/45, median one call), and all session policies were perfect. The surprise is the ablation: bare stateless sessions, no history and no worked examples, also scored 240/240 steps with 20/20 intact end states. The examples block that rescued sonnet (13/20 without it) is not load-bearing on the frontier tier; it is cheap insurance for every tier below it, and it stays shipped. Fan-out remains the honest boundary, now with a third mitigation profile: opus raised the floor to 80 to 89% but still left a third of the 7-plus-target view tasks partially covered, so the app-side decomposition fence stands unchanged at every tier.

sections.eyebrow: Study AE · hatch calibration + the resume loop
sections.title: Only the frontier knows when a question is the right answer
sections.takeaway: Study AC left two fears on the record: that the escape hatch would tax clear requests with unnecessary questions, and that an ask might be a dead end. Study AE measured both on a five-level ambiguity ladder (precise, indirect-but-unique, discretionary, ambiguous-referent, missing-info; every level's defining property unit-validated) with the shipped NEED-INFO sentence frozen verbatim, plus 135 resume cells where the harness answers the model's question in plain text. Both fears refuted at ceiling: zero false asks in 90 clear-request cells with solve rates identical to the no-hatch control, models edit "make it punchier" rather than interrogating the user about wording, and the ask-answer-patch loop closed 135 of 135 with zero re-asks and zero wrong integrations. An ask is a reliable two-turn solve, so reply paths can ship with confidence. The gate still fails, and the failure is the finding: when a singular request matches exactly TWO visible nodes, opus-4.8 asks 15/15 and names both candidate ids every time, while sonnet and gemini ask 1/15 each even with the hatch present. They resolve the ambiguity unilaterally instead, in different ways: sonnet edits BOTH matches, gemini silently picks one. The mechanism is textual: the registered sentence covers information that is "not visible in the view," and an ambiguous referent is entirely visible. The frontier tier generalized the rule's intent; the mid tiers applied its letter, the same literalism profile Study AA measured on conflicting specs. Guidance: on the frontier tier the hatch now covers absence AND ambiguity; below it, app-side disambiguation (unique references, deterministic enumeration, selection grounding) remains the only defense, and the obvious multiplicity amendment to the hatch sentence stays unshipped until a registered test passes it.

table.summary: Data table: outcomes by level, arm, and model

sections.title: Saying the goal out loud doesn't make it yours
sections.takeaway: One clause in the shipped session-notes rule had been inferred rather than measured: restate a goal from the memo in your own words before a goal-directed rewrite. The hope was that forced verbalization would also rescue Study V's sharpest loss, where a model shown the node its goal lives in reads it and still writes measurably less focused prose (117 of 120 judged losses). Study AF measured the clause with Study V's full protocol: both judges re-passed their 50-pair calibration gate before any verdict, 270 contemporaneous edits (all mechanically valid), each restate arm judged against a same-batch explicit-goal control in both presentation orders. The view-side hope is dead, without a single win: 0 wins, 79 losses, 11 ties pooled across three editors including opus. And the failure is not disobedience. GOAL-line compliance was 30 of 30 in every cell: every model read the mission node, restated the thesis accurately in its own words, and then wrote the off-goal paragraph anyway. Verbalization is not the active ingredient; where the goal comes from is. On the memo path the clause measured neutral under the registered primary judge (parity on all three editors) with a disclosed sensitivity dissent toward mild harm (gemini 1 win to 13 losses, opus 5 to 15 under the second judge), and where Study V's bare memo had beaten the control outright on sonnet, memo-plus-restate merely ties. The benchmark's recommendation: remove the clause. The memo itself keeps its goal-carriage parity, contemporaneously replicated here; the ceremony on top of it does nothing measurable. Views carry values, memos carry goals, and no prompt ritual converts one into the other.

sections.title: Perfect to the cap. At the cap, the goals die first.
sections.takeaway: Every study that shipped the session-notes memo measured it at three to six notes; the shipped implementation caps it at twenty, with a normalize step that silently drops the excess. Study AH filled it up. Below the cap the memo is flawless at scale: recall of any note from a FULL twenty-note memo scored 15 of 15 per model at every position (no burial: first, middle, and last notes all perfect), unprompted rule application from a twelve-rule memo was 15 of 15 per model with zero cross-note contamination, and the agent's full-replace update was lossless wherever the update fit, 60 of 60 clean at ten and nineteen notes with the requested edit landing 90 of 90 alongside. Then a twenty-first declaration arrived at a full memo, and a note died in all 30 cells, silently. The victim was a goal note every single time, on every model. The mechanism is structural: the block renders facts, then rules, then goals, so goals are always the tail of the list, and both loss modes eat the tail: opus over-sent twenty-one notes all ten times and let the shipped clamp keep the first twenty; gemini and sonnet usually pruned a goal themselves. Study V measured goals as the one thing only the memo can carry, which makes this the sharpest possible failure ordering: at capacity, the memo sacrifices its most irreplaceable cargo first, with no error and, in the over-cap cases, no model decision at all. The fix is application-side and filed: evict the oldest fact deterministically instead of clamping, never the goals tail, or surface memo-full to the user; prompt-side mitigations stay unshipped until measured. Below the edge, note-count is a provably safe budget.

sections.title: The obvious fix, measured: it helps exactly where we don't ship
sections.takeaway: Study AE left an obvious fix on the table: the shipped ask sentence covers what the model cannot see, so ambiguous references (visible, but two of them) slipped through on the mid tiers. One added sentence covering requests that match more than one node looks like it must work, and this series has now caught two obvious-looking clauses doing nothing (the priority meta-rule in AA, the restate ceremony in AF), so the clause was measured before anyone shipped it: amended sentence versus the shipped one, re-run contemporaneously, across the full five-level ladder on three models. The results split three ways. Sonnet is completely rescued: 3 of 15 asks became 15 of 15, every ask naming both candidate ids, with its silent edit-both habit gone. Gemini improved enormously, 0 of 15 to 11 of 15, but stopped one ask short of the registered detection bar, and its four residual failures all silently edited BOTH matches; the clause converted its coin-flips into asks or edit-boths, never back into correct restraint. And the clause taxed nothing anywhere: zero false asks in 90 clear-request cells, solve rates identical to control, hard boundaries undisturbed. The one cost signal lives on the tier we actually ship: opus, already perfect on ambiguity with the shipped sentence alone, started interrogating discretionary requests slightly more often under the amendment (asks on "make it punchier" cells rose from 2 of 15 to 5 of 15, not significant, but the only movement anywhere). So the registered gate fails by a single ask, and the practical verdict is sharper than a pass: the clause stays unshipped on frontier surfaces, where it buys nothing and whispers a cost; it is a large, free, but partial improvement for sub-frontier deployments; and app-side disambiguation remains the actual contract at every tier. Knowing when a question is the right answer keeps measuring as a capability that prompting approaches but does not close.

sections.title: The discourse gap closes on every tier; the visibility clause bites
sections.takeaway: One border of the ask-path map was never tested: Study X's discourse construction, where "undo that" against a carrier-less editor failed 0 of 144 with every failure a valid silent guess. The shipped ask sentence arguably covers it (a dangling referent is "not stated in the request"), so Study AG pointed the sentence at it: the carrier-less control, the control plus the shipped hatch, and the last-edit echo plus the hatch, across three models and 1,296 session steps. The control replicated Study X to the digit. With the hatch, 138 of 144 silent guesses became questions, on every tier, and the asks show genuine recognition: "the request refers to 'that same node' from a prior instruction, but no such node is identified." Unlike ambiguity, which only the frontier tier notices, the discourse gap is letter-covered, and every model protects itself. Then the tax check failed on all three models, and the ask texts locate the mechanism precisely. With the echo supplying everything (the node id, the key, both values), models still asked on roughly 70% of anaphora cells, quoting the echo's own node id while refusing to proceed because that node "is not visible in the current view." An anchored patch needs only the id; the echo-without-hatch arm solved 48 of 48 under identical views. This is the sentence's visibility clause colliding with skeleton views: the rule's letter says an unseen node warrants a question, so a fully specified, solvable edit becomes an interrogation. Ordinary steps in the same arm, whose views carry their targets, produced zero false asks in 288 cells. The guidance sharpens into a dependency: the hatch's zero tax is conditional on the focus-ids contract. Views that cover every mentioned node make the hatch free (measured three times now); outline-style protocols need target-carrying views, a self-serve view tool, or a re-scoped sentence that gets its own registered test first.

sections.eyebrow: Study AJ · the correction loop in isolation
sections.title: The error message didn't matter
sections.takeaway: Returning barkup's structured validation issues verbatim has been a design commitment in every arm of this series, the closing instruction of playbook guideline 01, and standing guidance in the production codebase, and it had never once been an experimental variable. Study AJ isolated it. Because correction loops rarely trigger naturally (first-pass validity runs 84 to 99 percent), the loop was seeded: the known-correct patch for each task was corrupted by a registered operator (dangling ids, missing fields, malformed op kinds, bad placement anchors, unknown attributes), injected as the assistant's own prior turn, and confirmed to fail the shipped applier. Then exactly one feedback message went back, the only variable in the study: the full structured issues, bare issue codes, or nothing but "the anchored patch was invalid." The result is parity. Opus recovered all 45 seeded failures in every arm, including from the bare sentence. Gemini scored an identical 42 of 45 in all three arms, and the three misses were the same cells every time, all in the one genuinely hard class (bad placement anchors); feedback quality changed nothing. Sonnet showed the only gradient, 45 to 44 to 42, not significant. Told a patch failed, models simply re-derive the correct edit from the task and the tree. One nuance runs in bare feedback's favor: its extra failures stayed visibly invalid rather than becoming plausible wrong fixes, so thin feedback does not even push toward silent errors. The commitment survives with its rationale corrected: return the issues verbatim because it costs nothing and makes correction logs humane for the people debugging them, not because the loop depends on it. Disclosed caveats: seeded single-op corruptions are a constructed proxy for organic errors, and recovery was single-shot where the shipped loop allows three rounds, which would only narrow the gap further.

sections.title: The fix works where it can, and the frontier tier invented consolidation
sections.takeaway: Study AH found that a twenty-first declaration at the memo's full cap always kills a note, and the victim is always a goal. The production fix shipped within a day: an app-side eviction that runs before the truncation clamp and removes the oldest fact, then the oldest rule, and never a goal. But shipped-in-response-to-a-finding is not the same as measured, so Study AK applied the Study AB standard and re-ran the injury site with the tool handler as the only variable: the old silent clamp as a contemporaneous control, the eviction pipeline as the treatment. Three results. First, the mechanical guarantee is perfect: in all 19 cells where a model sent an over-cap list, the pipeline admitted the new note, evicted only the oldest fact, and preserved every goal — zero contract violations. Second, the injury closes where the fix can reach it: goal survival at the cap edge went from 0 of 10 to 10 of 10 on opus and 0 to 6 of 10 on sonnet, while the control arm replicated the original injury almost to the digit, every victim still a goal. Third, no new damage: 60 of 60 updates below the cap passed through untouched. The honest boundary was pre-registered and held exactly: the app cannot restore a note the model pruned before sending, and sonnet pruned 4 of 10 and gemini 6 of 10 cap-edge cells client-side, victims still goals — so below the frontier tier the guarantee covers the clamp pathway, not the model's own editing. A prompt-side fence for the prune pathway is filed for future measurement rather than shipped untested. And one unregistered moment worth the price of the study: told via the eviction notice that its update had cost a note, opus alone called the tool again with an eleven-note memo carrying all twenty-one facts, rules, and goals — it consolidated the memo's content into fewer sentences rather than accept a loss. The regression suite now guards the cap edge permanently: goal-safe eviction on the opus baseline, with a hard zero on goals evicted by the pipeline.

sections.title: The gate fails on a moved baseline — and unproven does not ship
sections.takeaway: Study AK left one pathway open: the app-side eviction cannot restore a note the model pruned before sending, and the mid tiers pruned goals client-side in 4 to 6 cells of ten. AK's interpretation table filed the obvious candidate — one prompt sentence forbidding self-eviction ("never drop or trim an existing note to make room; the app decides evictions") — for measurement before shipping, and Study AL is that measurement, with the prompt rule as the only variable against the AK-eviction arm as its contemporaneous control. The fence looked right everywhere the gates could not see: pooled client prunes fell 5 to 1, goal survival rose to 10 of 10 on sonnet and 9 of 10 on gemini, all sixty under-cap updates stayed untouched, and the sentence cost nothing — the models were already sending complete lists; the fence changed which notes survived, not how many tokens moved. But the pre-registered significance gate failed at p = .219, for a reason nobody registered: the control arm did not replicate its own three-day-old baseline. Sonnet's prune rate halved (4 of 10 to 2), gemini's too (6 of 10 to 3) — same prompts, same corpus, same handler, temperature 0, the largest drift the series has caught between two measurements of the same construction. Against a five-prune pooled baseline, ten cells per tier cannot clear the bar. So the published verdict is deliberately double-edged: the registered reading ("the prune pathway is not instruction-closable") overstates what this run measured, and the honest reading — unproven, not disproven — still ships nothing, because unproven does not ship. What the study bought instead is sharper than a pass: the client-prune baseline itself is unstable week to week, which is the strongest argument yet for the filed alternative — an update shape that cannot express omission at all, so the guarantee stops depending on tier behavior holding still. Two smaller facts round it out: opus pruned for the first time in the series (a fact, not a goal — its goal safety stayed perfect), and consolidation-on-notice recurred, two sightings in two studies.

sections.title: The notice learned to ask for everything back
sections.takeaway: Twice in two studies — both times unregistered — opus answered an eviction notice by re-sending the memo compressed into fewer sentences carrying all twenty-one needles: told a note had died, the frontier tier invented lossless consolidation rather than accept the loss. Study AM measured the mechanism instead of admiring the anecdote. The intervention surface was chosen by the series' own results: Study AL had just measured the agent-prompt-rule surface failing at the cap edge, and Study AB long ago measured the opposite surface — app-authored text at the point of injury — fixing what buried text could not. The eviction notice is exactly that surface, and it arrives attached to the event that makes it actionable. One sentence appended to it, the notice string the only variable, on a fresh seeded forty-task cap-edge corpus: the same facts, rules, and goals rewritten into fewer, denser notes; nothing needs to be lost. The result is the cleanest pass in the series: opus lossless recovery went from 3 of 40 spontaneous to 40 of 40 invited (p ≈ 3×10⁻¹¹), every planted needle surviving with kind fidelity 800/800 — facts staying facts, rules staying rules, goals staying goals through the rewrite — zero degraded cells on any model, zero re-add churn, and about 570 extra output tokens for the recovery call. The sub-frontier tiers ignore the invitation entirely and harmlessly, so the sentence ships ungated. It shipped as v3.215.0 the same day. And the pass settles a design question beyond the cap: any future omission-proof update protocol now has a measured lossless behavior to beat, because merge-style semantics would structurally break the very consolidation this study just turned into a guarantee.
